core: What this topic is: a note to readers that clinical content in this curriculum carries general-education depth, not professional advice
Why the note exists: clinical material can look like guidance even when it only informs
What the curriculum does: teaches concepts and vocabulary
What it does not do: give dosing, treatment, or diagnostic advice
The reader's role: learn, then verify with professionals
This lesson as the marker readers can recognize
The honest framing: knowing the limits of a resource is part of using it well
supporting: Personal health literacy (CDC definition): find, understand, use information to inform health decisions
Source evaluation questions: who runs the site, purpose (inform vs. sell), who pays, balance, sources and dates
Patients as active members of the care team and asking providers or pharmacists questions
Keeping a written list of medicines and reading labels
outOfScope: All clinical content: vital signs, medications, infection control, assessment, and related topics belong to sibling lessons
Any dosing, treatment, or diagnostic guidance of any kind
Professional practice standards, licensure, or scope-of-practice law
Technical evaluation of research studies (owned by research-literacy and evidence-based-practice lessons)

claims.claim: Personal health literacy is the degree to which individuals can find, understand, and use information and services to inform health-related decisions.

Good starting points for health information are sites run by federal government agencies, medical schools, and large professional or nonprofit organizations, and good material is balanced, research-based, and shows its sources and dates.
A key evaluation step is asking what a resource is for — to inform, to sell, or to persuade — because purpose shapes how the material should be used.
Readers should verify personal health decisions with qualified professionals, for example by asking the provider or pharmacist questions about a medicine and keeping a written list of medicines.
Patients who take an active part in their own care tend to get better results, and being an involved member of the care team helps prevent errors.

An educational resource that teaches concepts is not a substitute for professional advice; knowing what a resource is for is part of using it well, and this lesson is the curriculum's plain-language marker of that boundary for its clinical lessons.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Health information varies widely in quality, and some sites blur the line between informing and advising (or selling).
positions: MedlinePlus advises evaluating who runs a site, its purpose, who pays for it, and whether the content is balanced and research-based, treating government, medical-school, and professional or nonprofit sources as stronger starting points.
Business-funded sites may present product-friendly material as neutral information, which is why purpose and funding are part of the evaluation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson applies the same evaluation habit to itself: readers are told plainly what the curriculum is for (education) and what it is not for (professional advice), and are directed to verify personal health decisions with qualified professionals.

sourceRecords.title: Evaluating Health Information
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports the source-evaluation claims of this note: good health information is found on sites run by federal government agencies, medical schools, and large professional or nonprofit organizations; evaluation questions include who runs the site, the site's purpose (inform vs. sell), who pays for it, whether information is balanced and based on research, and whether sources and dates are given. Used to frame 'knowing what a resource is for is part of using it well.' Facts synthesized in original wording; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Patient Safety (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Registry-verified read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Used for the 'reader's role' framing — informed participation, not self-treatment. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
